speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, I would like to call the attention of the Prime
Unopposed Motions for Papers

Minister to a request which I made yesterday regarding the production of returns to parliament. I have in my hand a return comprising fifty-two pages, which I must hand back to the clerk of the house. My request yesterday was that arrangements might be made in the departments by which a duplicate could be made of these returns at the time the original is being made, and the duplicate could be given to the member of the house who had moved for the return. It would save lots of trouble, would entail no additional labour, and would be a great convenience to members of the house. The same thing is done with questions now.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REQUEST THAT RETURNS TABLED BE PREPARED IN DUPLICATE
speechtext: So far as my inquiries go, I am satisfied that this has never been done before, and it does involve an amount of extra labour. Whether a new departure is to be made now depends entirely upon the view of those who have to be responsible for the doing of it, I suppose. I shall look further into the matter and advise the hon. gentleman, but why this sudden departure should be made now-

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REQUEST THAT RETURNS TABLED BE PREPARED IN DUPLICATE
speechtext: Because it is better business, and we know that this government wants that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REQUEST THAT RETURNS TABLED BE PREPARED IN DUPLICATE
speechtext: These returns come from many different departments, and if an extra copy is to be made it would have to be filed either with the clerk or with the keeper of these records, because equal facilities should be offered to all who desire to see the returns. I have frequently desired to see a return myself which was in the hands of someone else at the moment. If two copies of the return are to be made, then, of course, they should be available to all members of the house who wish to see them, rather than the extra copy being given to the member immediately concerned. If it is desirable to make an extra copy and the rules are altered to that effect, I suppose it can be done, but not for the purpose of giving the mover for the return the extra copy, because all members are interested in the return, and it would have to be made available to all. It well may be that one copy is not sufficient. We will look into the question and see whether we cannot make two, so that there will be two copies available for the use of the house.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REQUEST THAT RETURNS TABLED BE PREPARED IN DUPLICATE
speechtext: As I said, the practice of making a duplicate 'has been followed in regard to questions on the order paper. The answers are given in duplicate, and one copy is given to the member who put the question. I think the same practice might be followed with returns.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REQUEST THAT RETURNS TABLED BE PREPARED IN DUPLICATE
speechtext: Some of these returns are not made for weeks after the house rises. Hast year I recall one very long return comprising several hundred pages. We were working steadily on it, but it was not filed in the proper office until after the house had risen.

I find that on February 27, 1928, the Department of Public Works of the province of New Brunswick forwarded a certified copy of an order in council of that province undertaking to contribute one-third of the cost of this bridge on condition that the province of Quebec make a similar contribution and the Dominion of Canada a like contribution. No communication has been reecived from the province of Quebec to the effect that it approves of the proposed undertaking, and no further action has been taken by the Public Works Department. The estimated cost of the bridge is $1,300,000; that is not for a railway bridge, but purely a traffic bridge.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
On a matter of ' privilege, may I direct Your Honour's attention to a question which appears in yesterday's votes and proceedings under Notices of Motions and Questions, as follows:
Mr. Lafleche-On Thursday next-inquiry of ministry-
1.	On what date was Mr. Edward Tobin appointed senator?
2.	Did he possess the required financial qualification at the time of his nomination?
3.	Is it the intention of the government to make an inquiry in this matter?
4.	What division does he represent?
5.	Does he possess the necessary education?

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
May I say,
Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Mr. Tobin at the time of his appointment to the Senate had been a member of this House of Commons for something like thirty years, during which time he not only earned but enjoyed the respect of hon. members on all sides of the house. I know that at the time of his appointment to the Senate there were expressions from the other side of the house quite as appreciative towards him as many of those that came from his own side. I submit that a question such as the one I have read should not be permitted to appear in the votes and proceedings or to appear upon any
order paper of this house. In the first place, it constitutes a reflection upon a member of parliament, a most offensive and uncalled-for reflection. In the second place, as Your Honour knows, each house is the custodian of its own rights and privileges and dignities, and if questions are to be asked with respect to any hon. member of the Senate, it is in the Senate chamber and by members of that body that the question should be asked. I feel quite sure that Your Honour's attention could never have been directed to this question, for I am certain that had such been the case you would not have permitted the question to appear.
While on this subject, may I say that looking over many of the questions, it would almost seem that a not inconsiderable number owe their origin to some personal vendetta rather than to a desire to secure information in the public interest. I suppose there is no way to control the questions that may be asked, and certainly I for one would not wish to see the rights of any hon. member of this house restricted or circumscribed in the matter of securing ample information on any question; but, after all, the House of Commons is a body of representative gentlemen, I hope, and there must be something in the nature of amenities between the different sides of the house which it would be well to observe with respect to matters of this kind. If I may make a respectful suggestion, it would be that Your Honour, as the presiding officer of the house, take occasion to have the Clerk of the House confer with Your Honour in regard to questions that seem on the face of them to be of a questionable character, and at least have them withheld until there has been opportunity for some consultation with respect to them. I hope Your Honour will rule immediately that this particular question should not appear upon any order paper of this house, first on the score that it concerns an hon. member of the Senate and secondly because it is of a most offensive character.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree entirely with
the remarks of the leader of the opposition. What he has said applies perhaps with equal force to both sides of the house. The present instance is not a case of the pot doing more than calling the kettle black. The other day my attention was directed to a question, but the question was on the order paper and any possible injury resulting from its appearance thereon had already ensued. If I so desired there are two questions at least to



Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
which I might refer which would be better left off the order paper. The point is, however:	Who is to determine how a question
is to be kept off the order paper? The hon. member files his question and in the ordinary course of routine the clerk places it on the order paper. As I understand the procedure, the Speaker does not or need not see it until the following day, when he has the opportunity of seeing it in the votes and proceedings Which it is his duty to sign.
The particular question in the votes and proceedings to which my right hon. friend opposite has just referred is one that need not be discussed at all, for the simple reason that this house has no jurisdiction in the matter. Had the question appeared on the order paper I would have answered it at once by directing the attention of Mr. Speaker to the fact that this was a matter affecting the Senate and with which the Senate alone could deal. However unless the Speaker had given permission I could not strike the question off the order paper once it had been placed thereon. I wholly agree with the right hon. gentleman that a question which affects another branch of parliament and which clearly is not a proper question to be asked in this house should not appear on the order paper. I think that point is fairly clear. As to the other aspect of the question, namely whether or not good taste and other considerations which should weigh dictated the asking of it, I am afraid that the clerk has no option, that he could not say that the question should not appear on the order paper.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has,
though.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext: The Prime Minister does not see the questions until after they are placed on the order paper.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext: He has enough to do.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
He has a duty as leader
of the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
The Prime Minister has
no duty with respect to the order paper until it is before the house; then he has. I think my hon. friend is not quite fair when he says there is a responsibility upon the Prime Minister before the questions appear on the order paper and the order paper is before him.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext: Quite right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
With respect to matters
which do appear on the order paper he then has a responsibility, and a very great one.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I withdraw that remark,
Mr. Speaker; I quite agree that the Prime Minister has nothing to do with it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
My right hon. friend
would be the first to say, as I would have said when leader of the opposition, that after all, the order paper is the sheet anchor of the opposition. The Prime Minister has no more to do with making up the order paper than any other hon. member of the house. If he had it would be a very sad day for representative institutions. I put it that way because I felt my remark would be appreciated by my hon. friends opposite. I felt perfectly certain they would realize there are so many questions that offend against the judgment of the Prime Minister that the order paper would be bereft of many indications of the contentions that hon. members sometimes make. At any rate the obligation of the Prime Minister begins the minute the order paper is before the house at the opening of the sitting. He must see to it on behalf of the house, and not on behalf of any one party, that it does not offend against the traditions of the house, the amenities of debate or the decencies of life. I think my hon. friends will not say that in any instance have they seen any indication on my part that the order paper of this house should not be of the character I have indicated. I have not had long experience-only a few months, but at least I have a great regard for the traditions of parliament; sometimes my friends say I have entirely too much regard for them. At any rate I assure the house that as long as I am in power I shall endeavour not to be an unworthy successor of those who have preceded me concerning the regard the house should have through the Prime Minister for maintaining the traditions of the house as reflected in the order paper. I cannot, however, undertake any responsibility antecedent to questions appearing on the order paper; when they do appear I shall endeavour to discharge my duties to the best of my ability.
I wholly agree that the question to which attention has been directed should be stricken from the records of the house. I do not know how it is to be done, once it has been placed thereon, unless the Clerk of the House arbitrarily but properly takes the view that the question concerns another chamber over which this house has no jurisdiction and with respect to Which its rights to criticize can arise only by proper parliamentary action and in the manner prescribed by constitutional procedure.

Imperial Conference

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
I wish to
thank the Prime Minister for his remarks. It is a great satisfaction as well as a pleasure to know that we are in entire agreement on a m'atter of this kind. I agree that the responsibilities of the Prime Minister should not be added to, but might I mention to him with respect to this matter of questions that there is a procedure which I think the clerk legitimately might adopt, and a procedure which would be appreciated by all hon. members of the house. When a question comes before the clerk which obviously from its nature is certain to occasion comment because of its offensive personal character he might bring it to the attention of one or other of the leaders or of the Speaker so that His Honour might confer with the hon. member asking the question before it is placed in printed form on the records of the house. On one occasion quite recently the clerk directed my attention to a question asked by an hon. member on this side of the house with respect to an hon. member on the opposite side and asked me if I thought the question as asked .would serve any useful purpose or if it was a desirable or proper question. I asked him to allow the question to stand a minute or two and I would communicate with the hon. member in whose name the question was to appear. As soon as I spoke to him the matter ended. The question had been placed under his name, having been handed in as many of the questions are. To my mind a practice of that nature would avert many unnecessary offensive and irrelevant questions.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING APPEARANCE ON ORDER PAPER OP UNNECESSARY IRRELEVANT AND OBJECTIONABLE QUESTIONS

It appears in a list of notices of motions and questions upon which action will be taken at a future date. As hon. members know, the course has been as a matter of routine, to hand the questions to the clerk of the house, and I have known of instances such as that described by the right hon. the leader of the opposition when the nature of a question has caught the attention of the clerk; suggestion having been made to the hon. member offering the question that it was not a proper one, it has thereby been prevented from appearing on the orders of the day. I shall see to it, whatever the procedure may be, that the question referred to, and which I quite agree with the Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition should never have appeared on the record, shall not appear on the orders of the day.

speechtext: On the orders of the day.

maintopic: IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING REPRESENTATION OF DOMINIONS AT OTTAWA MEETING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister a question which was yesterday asked in the British House of Commons and in reply to which the Secretary of State for Dominion affairs said the arrangements were in the hands of the Canadian government. Have all the dominions signified that they would attend the coming economic conference in Ottawa, and if so will they be represented by ministers?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: IMPERIAL ECONOMIC CONFERENCE
subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING REPRESENTATION OF DOMINIONS AT OTTAWA MEETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I reply subject to my
memory being defective because I had no notice of the question. The position, as 1 recollect at the moment, is that all the countries affected have tentatively agreed to the meeting being held in August this year, but since then events in Australia and New Zealand, as indicated by despatches received from the Prime Ministers of those overseas dominions, indicate the possibility of a general election in each country, and it may be that that will cause some little difficulty. The matter is now under negotiation in view of the information received during the last ten days from Australia and New Zealand.
As to the representation, that matter has not been determined so far as this government is advised by the governments affected, except that the two dominions in the southern seas indicated that each had hoped to have a very strong delegation, and were greatly disturbed by the present political situation. I think that is as fair an answer as I can give at the moment, but as soon as anything definite is settled having regard to the disturbed political situation to which I have referred, I will advise the house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, May 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bennett for committee of supply and thfe proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Reid.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was speaking of the grievances of the farmers of British Columbia by reason of the fact that we in that province have to pay twice as much for the hauling of grain to Vancouver
Grain Hates-Mr. Reid

as have people living in countries like Spain and Japan. I had come to that part of my address where I *fras pointing out that it certainly was unfair and unjust that we should be called upon to pay such high rates, and that this discrimination was acting as a barrier to the progress and welfare of the farmers of British Columbia. To-day our producers of eggs in that province are getting less than 10 cents a dozen, which is the lowest price that has been received in 40 years. The situation is becoming so serious that it is practically impossible for the poultry men and others in British Columbia to carry on. We have to bring in our grain from the prairies, and the high domestic rates are tending in large measure to force our farmers [DOT]off their holdings. My grievance is that not only are these excessively high freight rates bringing about this very serious condition of affairs, but that no action has been taken on the petitions that have been filed on behalf of the provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan against a decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners in the matter. This application has been before the board since September of last year, that is, eight months have passed without that appeal having been heard, and the delay is causing British Columbia heavy financial loss.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Was not the appeal heard?
Mr. PJ5ID:	Not since September of last
year; that is my information. Two very important things are required to help stabilize the poultry and dairying industries of British Columbia; greater markets abroad and cheaper grain at home. Cheaper grain would result from reducing our domestic freight rates to substantially the same level as the export freight rates.
If the export freight rates on grain from the prairies to countries like China and Japan, which grain is carried through British Columbia, are fair and equitable, then the rates on domestic grain to British Columbia are certainly excessive. On the other hand, if the rates for export are too low, and the railways are losing money on the traffic, why should British Columbia be called upon to carry the whole burden? Why should the burden be placed on grain and food destined for domestic purposes in that province? The hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) not very long ago said, that due to present traffic and other conditions it was a bad time to discuss the lowering of freight rates. Well, I say to the hon. minister that if the freight rates are not

adjusted so far as British Columbia is concerned, the volume of business is certainly going to be less than it is at present; and I believe it is good policy to encourage the volume of business to British Columbia by lowering these rates.
I am now going to move the following amendment, seconded by Mr. Donnelly:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Whereas on September 30, 1930, petitions in appeal from a decision of the Board of Railway Commissioners were filed by the representatives of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, praying for a hearing and decision on the claims therein set forth for a reduction of the domestic freight rates in effect within these provinces, and-

Did the hon. gentleman

No, I was giving the date of

What is the date of the

Whereas the delay in rendering such decision has brought about a condition of confusion and instability which has seriously affected the poultry and dairying industries of British Columbia as well as certain important interests in the other provinces. [DOT]
