speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening I greatly
sympathized with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid); this afternoon my sympathy is not quite so great. Last evening he was speaking for himself and the people of British Columbia; to-day he is endeavouring to speak for a party. Yesterday his amendment was an amendment which he had himself prepared; to-day it is the amendment of the Liberal party-the opposition. If he was greatly interested in this matter, if he was as sincere as he would have us believe, he would not seek to destroy this government for the purpose of asserting his position. If his motion carries, this government resigns; that is his interest in this question. I wonder if he knows just what the facts are, I wonder if he realizes that the

Grain Rates-Mr. Bennett
judgment he is discussing is the judgment which was delivered by the Board of Railway Commissioners in 1926? In accordance with the promise made in this house by the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) the Board of Railway Commissioners, being seized of the facts under the reference, heard evidence and gave judgment. That judgment was delivered in 1926; that is the reason I asked the hon. member for New Westminster as to the date of the judgment. The judgment having been delivered, an appeal was taken to the former government, which he now supports and whose mouthpiece he is in connection with this amendment, in his desire to assist British Columbia poultry growers, which appeal was heard in 1929. This hon. gentleman now asserts that there has been a delay, when the former government which he supported and which is now in opposition heard the appeal in 1929, before the general election. Although they had weeks in which to give judgment, no judgment was given; the Privy Council, as then constituted, vanished after the election of July 28, 1930.
That is the position, Mr. Speaker. Now the hon. gentleman seeks to destroy this administration with an amendment on going into supply, as a vote of want of confidence, because he says that since September, 1960, this government has not had an opportunity to hear this appeal. Because in a time of great economic distress and of great difficulties for governments; because with the Prime Minister and several members of the administration away during the months of October, November and December, this government has not been able to hear that appeal-which could not be heard while parliament was in session-this hon. gentleman asks that this government be destroyed. Is that fairness? Is that his sense of justice? Is that his sense of what you might call elementary fair play? Doubtless there were good reasons which members of the late administration will advance as to why they were not able to hear that appeal from the time the judgment was delivered in 1926 until 1929. I think I can give reasonably sound reasons why this government has not been able to hear that appeal. I may say for the information of the hon. gentleman that twice we had, amongst ourselves, tentatively concluded that we might be able to hear the appeal on a given date, but the pressure of other matters made that impossible. With the burden of government which is being carried at this moment; with falling railway revenues; with conditions as they are, we are now told that because between September,
1930, and to-day, with the session of parliament beginning on March 12, and with the Imperial conference and all the problems with which this government has to deal before us, this appeal was not heard, the house is of the opinion that an early date should be forthwith fixed for the hearing of the petition. That would have been quite all right, but if the amendment passes this government goes out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would be a calamity.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There are many Canadians who would think so, and I may say there are many Canadians who formerly supported the government of the right hon. gentleman who would think so also. Their numbers are increasing every day, for when they hear members of a former administration going to and fro saying they are so grateful that they have not these responsibilities, and how glad they are that they have not to carry this load, the people of the country know perfectly well their inability to carry it. If the people had not known that hon. gentlemen opposite might have been in power still.
That is the position with respect to the matter. I said last evening I had some sympathy with the hon. gentleman. Thirty years ago the problem which he has discussed in this house was a problem to which I gave some little attention. I always found it difficult to understand, as a new settler in western Canada, why it cost more money to bring freight to Calgary than to Vancouver, from eastern Canada. I always found it difficult to understand just on what basis the rate structure of the country was fixed, but I took the trouble to investigate the matter. The classic case in this connection is the Spokane case, which ultimately went to the supreme court of the United States. It is a very interesting study in the whole question of freight rate structures and of terminal rates, as distinguished from intervening local rates on freight. The position is this, that by universal practice in railway rate structures you have first a cheaper through rate to terminals than you 'have to intervening points on a mileage basis, and although railway legislation of most countries provides that there should be no discrimination, nevertheless the application of the general rate per mile on the distance covered by the cars laden with the freight is held not to be applicable where you have water competition at a terminal point.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And water competition only.
Mr. ^BENNETT: Permit me to amplify it in my own way. I am sure I am indebted
Grain Rates-Mr. Bennett

to my hon. friend, but I will have to proceed in my own way. Water competition is the factor that determines that terminal rate. So far have the courts gone in upholding that principle that it was held that freight rates to St. Louis were to some extent regulated in the United States by water carriage to points on the Pacific slope. Vancouver is a harbour, and is situated on the ocean. Therefore the water rate factor enters into the question of the Vancouver terminal rate, altogether apart from the factor of what you might call terminal rates. That is the determining factor in reality; the water rate and all that is involved in it really determines the terminal rate in this case.
That is the first point. The next point is this: There has grown up in the commercial world the application of the principle of export trade being carried on a free trade basis. I suppose hon. members who have followed the tariff with care will realize that from time to time items are introduced that permit of drawbacks with respect to commodities produced in the country for export. That is what is called the application of the free trade rule in export trade, so that all countries are on a parity with respect to export trade. Germany carried that principle to a very great length during the years immediately preceding the war. In England the same principle prevails with respect to tariff items affecting goods that were destined for export. In the United States of course it has been applied during all these years, as it is unnecessary for me to say to this house, and we have applied it in this country as well. So you have these two factors which determine the question of the rate charged by railways for the transportation of freights of various classifications between points in Canada to Vancouver. There are other factors which are of minor consideration, which I will not mention at the moment, because I would be only endeavouring to discuss in this house a matter which I think should be discussed before the tribunal created for that purpose.
Those principles were recognized in the judgments of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and may I point out to my hon. friend that in his zealous and enthusiastic support of his proposition perhaps he has overlooked the fact that this parliament is hardly the tribunal to deal with this matter. Yesterday he was asking parliament, or the government, having a majority in parliament, forthwith to direct the railways to carry freight at a price named, that is, without giving the rate but at what might be called the export rate or the through bill of lading rate for export. To-day he does not do that; he

only asks that there shall be further consideration by the privy council. Now let us analyse what is the position. This parliament has created a court of record known as the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. This is not a voluntary tribunal nor an association; it is a court of record, provided by statute in the exercise of our powers over matters of that kind. That is a court which has been established in the same way as the Supreme Court of Canada is established, or the exchequer court. It is presided over by a chief commissioner, with associate judges or commissioners, just as the Supreme Court of Canada has a chief justice and associate judges. That court has complete control and authority over all questions relating to the operation of railways, including the charges to be made for the handling of traffic. The word "traffic" of course is defined as meaning both the carriage of passengers and of inanimate freight. That tribunal having been created, we have endeavoured to the best of our ability to ensure it from interference by parliament. Why? Because parliament is composed of partisans. Whether we like it or not, we are all partisans and it is extremely difficult for any of us-

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not very much.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, it is so pleasing
to hear that there are non-partisans on the other side. They will not long remain so. May I point out, however, that it is because we are partisans that the very earnest endeavour has been made to ensure that we shall not sit as judges. The very problems to which my hon. friend has directed attention are problems for judicial determination; and the judicial determination of these problems depends first of all upon the evidence submitted, and, secondly, upon a due and proper appreciation of the relation of that evidence to the relief sought. You seek relief; the evidence is adduced, and the relation of that evidence to the relief sought must determine the judgment given by the board. The board, or the court-because it is a court-gives judgment. That judgment does not support the views which have been put forward by those who are interested- my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid) for example. There is a right of appeal to the governor in council-that is to say, a right of appeal to the partisans. There are those who think that this right of appeal should not exist. The reason it exists is probably that it is a remnant of the old power which, before the court was created, rested entirely in the governor in council. The administration of railway matters, freight

Grain Rates-Mr. Bennett
tariffs and everything connected therewith, was all in the hands of the governor in council, the partisan tribunal. Now, the privy council is a court in this instance, and to that court an appeal was made. My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Justice sat, if my memory serves me, in that court when it heard the appeal. The appeal was heard by the late government. It was heard in its entirety, and that council reserved judgment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I say to my right
hon. friend that I heard only part of the appeal. The first argument proceeded while I was away at the Dominions conference on legislation in London. I heard only a small part of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The ex-Minister of
Justice reminds me that he did not sit through the whole argument, which lasted a considerable time-there were adjournments. One of the members of this house, before he became a member, was present at that argument, and counsel engaged were eminent members of our profession. What happened? Judgment was reserved. But in the meantime an election was held and the court vanished. That means a new hearing, because while the personnel of the court is gone, the appeal still exists. It means, I say, a complete new hearing, for it cannot be taken up where it was left off.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The testimony is there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am speaking about
the appeal, and I say that it means a reopening of the matter in its entirety before council.
I just put it again to this house, and I put it to my hon. friend: Does he not think that the amendment he has proposed has served its purpose and should be withdrawn? Does he think it is fair to any body of men- suppose he were one of them-
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver). Will the Prime Minister give us the assurance that, so far as he is concerned, he will expedite the proposed hearing as much as possible after the close of the session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am coming to that; I think it is a highly proper question and, indeed, it was not necessary to ask it. On two occasions the government was of the opinion that it should fix a future date on which the matter could be heard; but considerations of moment came up that made it impossible to fix a date. It is the intention of the government, however, to hear that appeal just as early as it is possible to do so, consistently
with the duties of the administration while parliament is in session. We cannot hear it while parliament is in session. It is true we heard an appeal the other day. Why? Because the Board of Railway Commissioners was appealed to on a question which affected the interests of a city with respect to level crossings in certain areas. That matter had been taken to the Supreme Court of Canada, who had decided that there was no question of law to be considered, whereupon appeal was made to the privy council. They asked that the matter might be remitted back to the board with a view' to having that body hear the evidence on a point with respect to which they said they had not been afforded the opportunity which they would have liked. The privy council limited their right to that one particular. It was admitted by counsel that there was no question of law involved, but it was felt there v'as a question respecting the equitable administration of the act. An opportunity was therefore given to have the matter considered.
I may say to the house that this government will not-unless it is a case in which a palpable error has been made that requires only an ' insignificant exercise of power-undertake to deal with these highly technical matters. I do not regard the Privy Council, either as at present constituted or as it has been in the past, as fitted by training to determine these questions. There is a body of men appointed for that purpose, trained men who have their experts to assist them. And if it is clear or reasonable from the appeal-one cannot anticipate the judgment -that the matter should be reconsidered, that, of course, will be done. It requires no direction or order of the house to bring that about. But I should be unfair to the government and to the country if I were to go further than to say that the matter is one of very considerable importance to the Dominion. And it is of more than considerable importance to those directly affected. My hon. friend must always bear in mind, however, as I learned so long ago myself, that it is easy to put one side of a case without sometimes thinking of the other side. I am sure he will learn, as most of us have done, that before the tribunal equal opportunity is afforded all, and the testimony is sifted with a view to determining the action to be taken in the light of the facts which are elicited from witnesses under oath, as occasion may necessitate. Thereupon judgment is given, based upon a due and proper appreciation of the facts and their implica-
Grain Rates-Mr. Bennett

tions. And this will be done with respect to the matters to which the hon. gentleman has referred.
I assure this chamber-it is a commonplace-that no government desires that there should be occasioned, in the transportation of commodities, delays greater than the Canadian people should bear. On the other hand, no government desires that this service rendered by the transportation companies should be provided at a loss. Now, between these two principles there must be a medium, and that medium determines the freight rate, that is to say, a fair compensation for the service rendered. It is difficult sometimes to arrive at that rate. I wonder whether hon. members realize just what the effects of modem conditions have been upon the revenues of transportation companies, of buses, and of mechanical transportation of all kinds. When later on the house has to consider the relation of these facts to our own properties, it will have perhaps a clearer appreciation of all that is involved in the work of preparing, understanding, appreciating, sifting and analyzing testimony to determine properly the problem to which the attention of the house has been directed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Merely with a view to expediting the matter, would it be possible for the present privy council to accept in a measure the evidence and arguments which were presented to the former privy council? I realize that further evidence might be desirable because of changing conditions, but would it not be possible for the present privy council to take advantage of the work that has already been done?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not any doubt that any privy council that hears this must take advantage of the work that has been done, but whether or not, in the light of present-day conditions, the matter could be then decided without further reference to testimony, and arguments or representations of council, I cannot antecedently determine.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I realize there are changed conditions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. It is now five years since the judgment of the board.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am referring to the hearing before the privy council in 1929.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Clearly the answer to that is in the negative. The personnel having disappeared, the body continuing, the new personnel must hear the arguments unless they are submitted in writing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A
different court and probably different advocates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member for Vancouver Centre will recall the decision of the English courts that the death of a judge necessitates a trial de novo. There may be an agreement between the parties affected as to a method to pursue whereby part of the representations previously made might be considered.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is all a matter of record.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I just want to direct the attention of the Prime Minister to an opinion which was given by the former deputy minister of justice, Mr. Newcombe, to the effect that in these appeals the privy council exercises administrative rather than judicial functions. I happened to come across it at page 124 of Beauchesne, and I thought it was pertinent to the question of my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am much obliged to the hon. member for Hants-Kings. I am well aware that the distinction between administrative and judicial with respect to appeals to the privy council from the Board of Railway Commissioners or other bodies, is not very clearly defined. There is a distinction, perhaps philosophic, but nevertheless the privy council are quasi-judicial if they are wholly administrative, and if they are administrative they are partly judicial. They could merely as a matter of administration decide to refer a matter back for rehearing; but if they undertake to adjudicate upon the merits of the application, their position would be judicial. That is the distinction between the judicial and the administrative function. If merely as a matter of administration they say: We will send this back for-further hearing and evidence, that is clearly an administrative power. If on the other hand, they say: Call your witnesses; we will hear this case de novo, or hear further testimony in addition to the written record, as the council might if they so desired, then clearly, before they arrived at a judgment, their function would be judicial.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would that be about the
practice in an appeal of that kind?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is competent under
modern practice to receive additional evidence in the Court of Appeals. Even in the House of Lords itself testimony is sometimes given before the final hearing. One of the most noteworthy cases in that regard is

Grain Rates-Mr. Mackenzie
one that originated with respect to a Nova Scotia ship. That however, is not a matter of importance.
I have endeavoured to put the case before the house as fairly as possible. I am not in any sense passing upon the merits of the controversy; that is not my business at the moment. All I know about it would be merely what I read in the newspapers, without having any opportunity to familiarize myself with it, and if I were familiar with it, I am speaking only in the absence of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) who is in Quebec to-day. If I did familiarize myself with it, I would then be endeavouring to pass judgment while one party to the proceedings had not been heard. By the terms of his motion my hon. friend is asking one party, the government, to vote that it is advisable that an early date should forthwith be fixed for a hearing, and knowing that we have a majority and have no intention of giving up office at present, he must realize we shall have to vote that it is not desirable so to do. Therefore this means that he does not want the appeal to be early heard.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very
much the central portion of the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). He commenced his lecture on an unfortunate note in seeking to impute motives to my good friend the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), who has brought this important question to the attention of parliament. On the contrary I submit that the hon. member for New Westminster has performed a public service to his own constituency, to his own province of British Columbia and to the Dominion of Canada by bringing this important question at this time to the attention of parliament. The Prime Minister in the course of his remarks said that parliament is not the tribunal to which this matter should be directed. I suggest to him that the Privy Council of Canada is the court of last resort so far as the people of Canada are concerned in all matters affecting freight rates, and the only opportunity we have to get the privy council to take action in these matters is to bring them to the notice of the privy council who sit opposite to us as ministers of the crown.
He said also that the late administration was somewhat dilatory in that it heard the appeal in 1929 and hand not rendered judgment up to the time it went to the country in July, 1930. I would suggest to him in that regard that we who are bringing this
matter to the attention of the house are not in the slightest degree concerned with the alleged dilatoriness or slackness of the former administration. We are here; our duty, our purpose is to see that the present administration takes action immediately or as soon as possible in regard to a final hearing and determination in respect to this matter and all other matters arising out of the circumstances to which reference has been made. Since the hearing in 1929 before the then privy council, the late administration, economic conditions in the Fraser valley have undergone a tremendously marked change, and I want to remind the right hon. gentleman and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), who knows the situation as well as I do, that to-day the removal of this differential between the export rate and the domestic rate is a matter of life and death to the poultry raisers in the Fraser valley, British Columbia. The situation is this, that you can export to-day to Kobe, Japan, or portions of China, our cheap grain, so that hens may be raised there and their eggs imported to undersell our eggs in the United Kingdom. The grain produced by the prairie provinces is permitted, by the present iniquitous structure of freight rates, to be sent to oriental countries, giving them an entry into a .$50,000,000 market so far as the egg importation business into the United Kingdom is concerned. This is done under the aegis and commendation of an administration that was ushered into office last July after preaching about the benefits of the home market.
The Prime Minister seemed to be very much perturbed because my hon. friend, in carrying out his duty, moved an amendment which the Prime Minister appeared to think imperilled the life of this precious administration. He knows full well, sitting in the seats of the mighty across the floor, that no amendment moved from this side of the house can at the present time endanger the life of that administration which he leads so splendidly. But we desire to bring this matter to the attention of the house in the only manner at our disposal, and so far as I am concerned, having received the promise of the Prime Minister that this matter, which is a question of life and death to the poultry raisers of British Columbia, will be brought to the attention of the government for hearing and decision as early as possible after the session, I am satisfied to have my colleague withdraw the amendment that has so terribly perturbed my right hon. friend at this time.
The difference between the 20-cent rate and the 41i-cent rate cannot be defended.
Grain Rales-Mr. Neill

We on this side of the house appreciate equally with my right hon. friend the Prime Minister the difficulties confronting our two great railway transportation systems at the present time. We know they are faced with falling revenues and a time of depression, a depression that is accentuated by the hopeless policies of the administration opposite. But while we appreciate the difficulties confronting our two great railway transportation systems, we are also acutely aware of the difficulties of the men who are struggling to live from one year's end to the other in the Fraser valley and other portions of British Columbia, and in other parts of the Dominion as well. There must be a middle course. Justice to the railway's, yes; but justice to our people in British Columbia also.
In conclusion, while I appreciate the constructive portion of the address of the right hon. Prime Minister I deprecate very much his opening and closing remarks. I thank him for the promise of an early hearing of the freight rate situation, and I am sure that with this promise my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid) will feel that he has achieved his purpose and will be prepared to withdraw his amendment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
While possessing neither the rugged persistence of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) nor the facile eloquence of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) I should like to say a few words on this motion, and I propose to adhere rigidly to the amendment because I wish to say something on the main motion after this is disposed of. Although he seldom agrees with me, I agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to some extent in his criticism of the amendment. My conception of an appropriate amendment would have been one somewhat similar to that he referred to, which would have been of a general character and would not have hesitated to allocate the blame for the delay equally between the past government and the present one.
On the other hand, the Prime Minister makes a great point of this being a motion of want of confidence. He is well aware that no matter in how mild terms the amendment had been framed, it would have been to all intents and purposes, under our rules, a motion of want of confidence.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Quite so; that is what
I said.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then it mattered very little
whether the hon. member made it a straight party question calling for a straight party

vote, or one dealing with the issue at large. The Prime Minister is also aware that owing to his assured majority it is only a mere matter of detail whether or not this is a motion of want of confidence. He is also aware that there is practically no other way of bringing a matter of this kind before parliament. There is probably many a man here who regrets that equally with myself, not only with respect to this question but other questions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is ample opportunity for discussion in committee of supply- on the estimates of the railway board, for instance.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It makes very little difference whether we discuss it on going into committee on the railway estimates or on the agriculture estimates.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I mean that there is ample opportunity when the house is in committee.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is so, of course, according to the precise rule, but we all know that if we want to get any serious attention to a matter we have to bring it up on a motion for going into supply, not on some particular item of the estimates when the discussion is strictly confined by the chairman, and properly so, to the item before the committee. A discussion in committee of supply has not the same effect and does not give you the same scope. To some extent I regret that this is a motion of want of confidence, but on the other hand I can recall that my hon. friends opposite made no complaint when I voted against the late government on a similar amendment a couple of years ago, and for the same reason, that I saw no other way of emphasizing the importance of the matter than by pushing it to a conclusion on a vote of want of confidence.
The question before us is an old one

I have under my hand a record of six occasions on which I have brought it up in the house- beginning with 1923 and the last occasion being ten days ago. I do not propose to inflict upon the house a rehash of my remarks on those occasions, but I should like to quote a greater authority perhaps than myself, Bulletin No. 80 published by McGill university, dealing with the hog export trade says:
There is one modification in connection with the present discussion which we unhesitatingly endorse. And it is this: That freight rates on grain and feed for domestic consumption should be as favourable as those on grain and feed for export.
A more favourable rate on export than on domestic grain amounts to a bonus on exports to that extent.

Grain Rates-Mr. Neill
I might also mention the question of mill feeds, bran and shorts, which I hope the Minister of Agriculture will take into his consideration. Our laws compel bran and shorts to be sold pure in Canada, but not outside Canada. The consequence is that adulterated shorts, with the low export rate, can be landed in Denmark at much lower rates than the pure shorts can be delivered in British Columbia, with the result that Denmark can compete with us in the bacon trade. The law should be altered so that adulterated shorts should not be allowed to be sold in either the domestic or export trade.
On a previous occasion, in 1928, I think, I dealt with this matter, and I referred to what I called the desperate condition of the poultry industry in British Columbia; I did not think it could possibly be any worse than it was then. I cited the case of one man with five thousand birds, who said:
Last month I shipped over 10.000 eggs, and I only received over the cost of the month's feed bill $14.20, for a month's work every day, including Sundays, 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
On the same occasion I made allusion to the fact that the products of the hen alone- not the poultry-brought in a gross revenue per year of something like 880,000.000. Hon. gentlemen will hardly credit that. Conditions have grown, I am sorry to say, much worse. I wish to quote a couple of short extracts from letters that I have received recently. One is from a gentleman who adheres strongly to the party in office, so this cannot be called an ex parte statement. He is a practical farmer, with 500 birds laying well, with 70 per cent extras, that is, high-class eggs. Here is his record for the. last four months from January to April. His feed bill, bought at best prices through a cooperative, for January was 880.10, and what did he got from the egg pool that month? He got $0.20 over his feed bill. In February he got 25 cents over his feed bill. In March he went behind $14.60. In April things looked up and he made a gross profit of $3.75. His total feed bill for the four months was $346.50, and he took in $342.10, so he only lost $4.40 on his four months' operations, and of course, all his work, seven days a week, as well as rent, depreciation, insurance, upkeep of buildings and all the other expenses. Then that man is expected to go to church on Sunday and sing a hymn, one line of which goes like this:	"Peace on earth, good will towards
men."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What would have happened had we not increased the duty on eggs nine cents a dozen last fall? He would have lost his farm.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He has lost it now, or it is on the way.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is living on his capital.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is not the only one.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would like you to take notice, Mr. Speaker, that the expression that this man is living on his capital has caused some amusement among hon. members on the opposite side of the house. If I may be permitted I shall quote a letter from another man. It is as follows:
Lower freight rates are the only hope I can see for the industry in this province and this includes the dairymen and swine breeders as well. If you need any figures on the poultry production costs, or the cost of producing eggs I would be glad to supply you. I enclose some quotations on feed showing how the present freight rates are as great as the cost of feed, f.o.b. Edmonton.
Enclosed are some price lists from a wholesale house in Edmonton. It shows that the ordinary stuff needed for chickens, Nos. 4 and 5 wheat, runs from $12.50 down to $9 for stuff which would be suitable for pig feed. The freight rate for that material is $10.80 per ton. In some cases the freight rate is actually more than the price of the feed. In addition to that $4 has to be allowed for sacking and grinding. That makes a total of $14.80, or about $3 a ton more than the original cost of the grain. No wonder the hon. members from the prairies are also kicking about the prices to them.
There is another aspect to which I wish to direct the attention of hon. members which I do not think has been mentioned before in this debate. On a previous occasion when I spoke in the house I set out the difference between the export and domestic freight rates; I figured the difference to be $3.80 a ton. Previous to that it had been $3.20 and now it is $4.10. For the sake of argument let us assume that it is right that the export rate should be higher than the domestic rate. In my opinion that is not right. Let us suppose that that would be a proper condition, and let us consider that since the year 1922 there have been two reductions in the export rate and no reduction in the domestic rate so that at the present time the spread is nearly double what it was previously. If the first spread could be justified certainly the last two could not be. At this time I wish to quote from the Province, a well known paper in the west.
Meanwhile, feeders, instead of using surplus wheat and barley from the Canadian prairies in their barns, are using Argentina or
1S0U
Grain Rates-Mr. Neill

American corn or imported prepared feeds of one sort or another. If the government of Canada desires to aid the prairie farmer in his distress-and there appears to be no doubt it does-*

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who says that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Province. The quotation
continues:
-it can aid him by making it possible for him to find a home market for that part of Ills crop which he cannot send abroad.
Of course it will help equally the consumer in British Columbia and in the eastern provinces as well. I fully agree with the remarks of the Prime Minister concerning the difficulty of a political partisan body-because that is what the Privy Council of Canada is -dealing with a matter of this kind. However that is at present the only means of redress we have. I suggest that the matter '*should be referred not to the privy council but to the supreme court, which is not a partisan body and which has more time, opportunity, facilities and experience in weighing evidence properly in a matter of that kind than has the privy council. The supreme court could not be accused of being partisan in its views. Mr. Speaker, perhaps I am wrong in saying so, but I think if these men would take the law into their own hands and break it, the matter would be brought more rapidly to a head than by any other means. If five hundred of the poultry men in the vicinity of my friend from New Westminster, under the guidance of their local cooperative association, were to buy a carload of feed from the prairies, and when it arrived if they were to pay the agent at the little station the export rate and then open the car and each *take a sack away from the car and decline to pay any more for it,-well they could not all be put in gaol.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would
direct my hon. friend's attention to the fact that they are not permitted to break the seal or to open a car until they have paid the freight rates. '

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suggest that they take the law into their own hands and break the seal after they have paid what they think would be a proper rate. Such action would bring the matter to a head and to the attention of the various courts of Canada. Five hundred men could not readily be put in gaol, and as I say their action would bring the matter to an immediate head. Such action would bring the matter before the public and receive its sympathy and attention. If such action were not considered practicable I would advise the cooperative association to sue the railway

company for the return of moneys. Such action could ultimately reach the Supreme Court of Canada. I think if any groups of fair size of any political party were determined to block the estimates to be considered in the house they would receive some satisfaction. However, at this time four or five men could not so block the estimates, because a few years ago, through the adoption of the forty-minute rule, we abandoned our right of free speech and sold our birthright for a mess of pottage. May I add that we did not get the pottage. At that time four or five determined men could have got some action. A man who would take such an attitude might be termed a bolshevik; it would be said that his action was absurd. Yet minorities have some rights under our laws. I wonder what advance would have been made on the Irish question in the old country if Irish members had not resorted to methods of obstruction. We would now be spending half our time listening to divorce bills had it not been for the action of my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). At the time his action may have been deemed a nuisance-it was a nuisance-but he got results. At last, as in the case of the importunate widow, we said, "Oh, fix the thing, for the sake of getting rid of it." That is the way the law was established. If a comparatively small number of men in this house said: "We are not going to vote money to carry on the business of Canada until we see more immediate prospect of action," they would get it. We do not expect the government to do the thing in a dlay. Before a promise of definite action however there should be no money voted. It would be wonderful to see how such a group of men would gain strength. Not only the little party itself but other people who are not in the party would say, "What is the trouble?" Eventually they would say, "It is right; why do you not deal with it?" Public sentiment would be aroused. The public would say, "These people are right; why do you not give them justice?"
I would like to mention one other point. Two or three hon. members from the prairies have been talking about two or three million dollars about which they are asking the government. They want to know whether or not the government has this money up its sleeve. Apparently the money was received from the sale of wheat in the years 1919 and 1920. There seems to be some doubt about it. They are talking about it, and they want it. Perhaps some day the British Columbia farmers will say, "We want a repayment of

Grain Rates-Mr. Barber
the money which has been taken from us illegally since this rate has been put into effect. On two occasions the export rate was lowered, but the domestic rate has not been lowered at all." We will be coming forward asking for a long overlooked redress. I am not referring especially to the present government. As I said the last time I spoke on it, the late government stalled on this question and the present government are stalling on it. That is the exact situation. Why do they do it? Is it because they do not wish to antagonize the railway interests, or what is it? I ask the question and leave it to anyone who can to answer it.
Most of the propositions which are brought forward in this house asking for reform or for the promulgation of certain policies are made with the idea and the contention that they will produce improved conditions throughout certain parts of the country. The matter at present under discussion however may be viewed from two angles. First, it is a matter of simple, common barefaced justice, and it has the further angle or inducement that it would prevent a whole industry from being wiped out. Hon. members can go along the roads through parts of British Columbia and see house after house standing empty. This man used to grow chickens; this man tried to make a living raising pigs, but he could not compete with Denmark, and so on. The acceptance of this amendment would prevent the wiping out of these industries. As I say it is a matter of equal justice to all. There seem to be double-barrelled reasons why the government should take action immediately. I would have liked to see the Prime Minister a little more emphatic in his decision that at an early date he would settle the matter. His suggestion seemed to be more in the way of sending the matter back to the railway board. However the railway board has already dealt fully with the matter and turned it down. If we could get a more emphatic assurance from the government I would be heartily in accord with the suggestion that the amendment be withdrawn.
Mr. HARRY J. BARBER (Fraser Valley): Mr. Speaker, representing a district perhaps more affected than any other in the province of British Columbia by the high domestic freight rates now prevailing, to which reference has been made this afternoon, I cannot let the opportunity pass without making a few remarks.
I agree with the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) that up to the close of the house last night I was very much in sympathy with the hon. member for New Westminster
(Mr. Reid), but when to-day he presented his amendment and injected party politics into the case I found myself unable to vote for the amendment. I repeat, I was quite in sympathy with- the hon. gentleman yesterday for he put up a good case and covered the ground thoroughly. He said that we have been somewhat negligent in bringing [DOT]this matter to the notice of the House of Commons in years gone by. I would remind him that it has been brought forward every session for the last five years to my knowledge.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In this connection I give
great credit to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). He is in a little different position from the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) because he has taken an independent stand. It was amusing to hear the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) rise in his place and with great indignation condemn the government for the serious condition of these industries in British Columbia. We had an election there last summer just the same as you had down here, and on that occasion hon. members should have heard the hon. member and others during the course of the campaign. To assist them they had the present right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). When he arrived in British Columbia his political friends and advisers told him, "Now, you will have to make some announcement with regard, to the freight rates question. The discriminatory character of the domestic freight rates is a very important issue here, and the election or defeat of a number of your supporters in this province will depend upon your announcement." The right hon. gentleman appeared in my constituency and also in other parts of the Fraser valley and made an announcement. I want the house to bear in mind that when he did so he was speaking as a member of the privy council before whom the question of these domestic rates was then sub judice. On a platform in the city of Chilliwack he said in effect: "This question of freight rates, I want to tell you ladies and gentlemen, we are working up to a successful decision, a decision that will be favourable to you. Now, I cannot go any further than that."

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Was that after the
hearing?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A decision had not been
given. It has not been given yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was after the
argument.
Grain Rates-Mr. Barber

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, after the argument
had been heard. On that platform in Chilliwack he spoke along these lines:	"Now,
send down this gentleman"-my opponent; I am going to say something about him later-"send him down and I am sure we can fix this matter up satisfactorily to you people." Mr. Speaker, please bear in mind that this was not the first time that the right hon. gentleman had made that statement. He came out to the coast in 1925 and visited Vancouver. This question of discriminatory domestic freight rates was then an issue; it has always been an issue in British Columbia-It is a very important matter to us and it was brought to his attention. In 1925 he said in effect: " The government that I represent fully realizes the seriousness of this condition, and we will proceed at once to fix it up." He came back in 1926 and again referred to the freight rates to this effect: "This is, we know, a very serious problem and one that must be adjusted immediately, and I promise you people that the Liberal party will get busy immediately after the election and will adjust this to the satisfaction of you people." But in spite of those promises in 1925 and 1926 nothing was done, and yet he comes back in 1930 with the same old story. Now, my friend from New Westminster brings down an amendment which involves a vote of want of confidence in a government that has not been in power more than nine months. Well, even if the government was a Liberal government, and I was in opposition, I do not think I would feel justified in supporting such a want of confidence motion. I do not believe that any member on this side of the house would do so. But I think the hon. member for New Westminster, being a fair-minded man, would not hesitate to vote want of confidence in the preceding government before whom this question was under consideration for nine years. During all that time they did nothing, they made not one cent reduction in the domestic freight rates. What happened? The hon. member for Vancouver Centre mentioned the name of the man who ran against me. I may say-

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did
not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, he called him by his first name.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No,
I did not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then I take it back. Perhaps it was the member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Hanbury). The hon. member for Vancouver Centre, as the house is aware,

for a short time occupied a position in the government of British Columbia. When this freight rates question was before the Board of Railway Commissioners, and before the privy council, it was brought to the attention of the Liberal government then in power at Ottawa that we had a Liberal government in power at Victoria under the leadership of the Hon. John Oliver-a particular friend, I believe, of the hon. member for New Westminster. What happened? They employed a legal gentleman to come down to Ottawa and present the case not only to the railway commission but to the privy council. Of course, the Liberal government in British Columbia thought that a Liberal lawj'er would appeal to the right hon. gentleman w'ho then occupied the position of Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The provincial government of which my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre was a member, employed this lawj'er.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is
not correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You were later.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is
correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I believe the hon. member was never reelected after appointment to the position.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was
always elected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Stick to the facts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is a fact. That
Liberal lawyer came to my riding and distributed copies of a newspaper from one end of the constituency to the other with the statement "I have worked for you for years and years for nothing; therefore I expect you will send me down as your representative." Immediately I got in touch with Victoria and received a copy of his account and found that the former Liberal government of the province had paid him $168,000 for his services extending over a period of less than six years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
May I
remark that I hope my hon. friend does not give the impression that he is referring to me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, no, I am referring
to your party in Victoria and to your party here as having some bearing on the case. The point I am making is that for nine years while we had the Liberal party in power here and the Liberal party in power in British Columbia, and a well-paid Liberal

Grain Rates-Mr. Veniot
lawyer was sent to Ottawa to appear before the privy council, not one cent reduction was made in the domestic freight rates that bear so heavily on British Columbia. Yet notwithstanding that long delay, this hon. gentleman from New Westminster now moves an amendment involving a vote of want of confidence in this government that has been in office only nine months, and his reason for moving the amendment is that in nine months-not nine years-the present government should have adjusted the matter I think this is unfair. As to the problem faring us, I agree with the hon. member for Comox-Al'bemi (Mr. Neill) and with the case as presented by the hon. member for New Westminster that the matter is serious, but I feel sure from the statement of the Prime Minister to-day and from statements which have been made by the Minister [DOT] of Agriculture that this matter will receive serious consideration at the hands of the government. I believe they understand the conditions which exist in our province and the problems facing us, and I am sure they will make every effort to solve it. As I said before, if this resolution had been left as it was placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) and brought in as it should have been brought in, I should have been only too glad to second the motion, but we find again the same old game, the injecting of politics into this question. That has been done by a few Liberals in British Columbia in every election, and this question made a political football. I will say, however, that the producers, the dairymen, the poultrymen and the . boards of trade of that province do not want this question thrown into the political arena. I think as citizens of that province, as business men, farmers and poultrymen we are all of one opinion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the hon. member be in favour of getting a favourable decision right now, in view of the conditions which exist at present?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am in favour of the privy council giving a decision at the earliest possible moment; I do not know whether that decision will be favourable or unfavourable. I know it took the government supported by my hon. friend a long time to deal with the question; it went over for a year, and there was no decision. It was Still under consideration when the election was held.
In conclusion let me repeat that I would have supported the original motion, for the purpose of educating some of the hon, members of this house and some of the people in
eastern Canada in one of the many problems faced by the people of British Columbia. In that province we have problems which are perhaps peculiar to us, and this is one of them. I think that would have been ' the proper way to bring up this matter, instead of using it as a weapon with which to attempt to destroy a government which has been in power only nine months, and which has not had time to consider the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not desire to take up much of the time of the house on this matter, and perhaps I would not have spoken at all had it not been that this matter affects the maritime provinces just as much as it affects the province of British Columbia. The domestic freight rate from west to east, from Winnipeg to the maritime provinces, is such that we in that section of the Dominion cannot take advantage of the opportunity to purchase wheat in order to develop the flour milling industry in the maritime provinces. If British Columbia has proper and reasonable grounds on which to ask for a lowering of the domestic rate in comparison with the export rate, we in the maritime provinces feel that we have an equal claim.
I should like to ask the government, in considering this matter, not to consider the application of British Columbia alone but to consider domestic rates generally throughout the Dominion of Canada. Now, when the price of wheat is so low, if we in the maritimes could take advantage of reduced domestic rates in order to purchase that wheat in large quantities, we would have established in the province of New Brunswick no less than two large flour mills to-day. I may say for the information of the house that in 1896 the provincial government of the day subsidized improved roller process mills for the manufacture of flour, intending thereby to encourage the growing of wheat in the province of New Brunswick. Quite a number of mills were established under that subsidy, but it was discovered that we could not raise wheat, owing to our climatic conditions, in sufficient quantities to warrant these subsidies 'being maintained. Lately a movement has been started in the maritime provinces for the establishment of one or two large flour mills in the city of St. John, but it has been found that the domestic rate on wheat from Winnipeg to the maritimes is so high that this wheat cannot be brought from the west. If a reasonable domestic rate could be given, the western farmers would find in the maritimes an increased market for their wheat andi
Grain Rates-Mr. Veniot

for their coarse grains as well. In that way both the western and the eastern provinces would benefit, and it is 'for this reason I am interested in the question now before the house, in the hope that the government may take our case into consideration. I know that without an appeal from the maritime provinces against a decision of the railway commission the privy council cannot deal directly with the maritimes, but in dealing with this whole question of domestic rates from Winnipeg to the coast I hope at the same time the privy council will direct the railway commission to deal with domestic rates from west to east, from Winnipeg to St. John and Halifax.
While I am on this question, there appears to be a misunderstanding as to the date cm which the appeal was heard by the privy council. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) stated that this matter has been standing for nine years, and that the Liberal government was dilatory in dealing with the matter. The decision of the railway commission was given in 1926. The appeal from that decision to the privy council was made in 1929.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was it not the hearing'that was held in 1929? I think the appeal was lodged some time prior to that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hearing was held in 1929. The appeal may have been lodged some time previous to that, but if hon. gentlemen will look up the records they will find that while one province was ready to proceed, another province was not ready, and in order to bring them together a date was fixed some time in September or October, 1929. Even that hearing was postponed at the request of some of the provinces, and the hearing did not actually take place until late in January, 1930. Parliament met on February 7, 1930, and during that session the former government had no time to deal with the appeal, so that no decision was given. If the reason, therefore, given by the right hon. Prime Minister this afternoon for the inaction of the present government since September is good, that reason has equal force in regard to the action of the former government. The former government did not hear the last presentation on the appeal until late in January, 1930, and it was not their fault. They were not to blame.
In conclusion, I should like to say a word with respect to this want of confidence motion. It was surprising to me that the Prime Minister should find fault with any one on this side of the house for moving a motion that might have the effect of a want of confidence in the government of the day.

The hon. member who has moved the amendment or motion, as the case may be, is a new member of the house. He is not supposed to know, perhaps as fully as old members of the house do, what the effect of such a motion might be. Yet in face of that, instead of being generous to the member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), the Prime Minister, to use a rather common expression, jumped down his throat. He reprimanded the hon. gentleman for bringing forward a motion that might entail the defeat of the present government. I was surprised, I say, that the right hon. gentleman should take that attitude, because in all the years I have been in parliament I have never known anyone to move more frequently- motions of want of confidence in an existing government than did the present Prime Minister when he was in opposition. If the hon. member for New Westminster proposed a motion which amounted to a want of confidence in the government, he was only following in the footsteps of the present Prime Minister; and when he does so the Prime Minister no doubt considers that the hon. gentleman is taking a safe course. The Prime Minister, I presume, feels that the hon. member is following the proper path when he follows his own example.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member knew what he was doing, then.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, even if he did know what he was doing, had he not a right to do it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then why reprimand him? Why impute motives to the hon. gentleman and say that he proposed the motion merely in order to place the government of the day in a trying position? Surely, with the majority which the Prime Minister has at his back to-day, he need fear no vote of want of confidence in this house. I knew he has a majority that will stand behind him through thick and thin no matter what he does so far as policies are concerned. I feel, therefore, that the hon. member for New Westminster should not have been taken to task by the Prime Minister. But it is not the first time that the Prime Minister has found pleasure in doing this, because it seems to be delightful to him to take to task new members on this side of the house. We old members who are used to the ways of the right hon. gentleman do not feel at all offended when he takes us to task. Indeed, we rather take it as a compliment when we are lectured by one who to-day stands up and blames us

Grain Rates-Mr. Weir (Macdonald)
for doing the very things which he did when he occupied the position of leader of the opposition-things which he did quite frequently and evidently with considerable gusto.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not particularly interested in what may have taken place in the past concerning this important matter; what I am interested in is what is likely to take place in the future Conditions have changed materially since the appeals and representations that were made in days gone by, so. that in my opinion it is essential that this important question should be reviewed again.
I congratulate the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) upon having brought this matter to the attention of the house. I wish particularly to congratulate him on the able manner in which he has presented the subject, and I would go so far as to congratulate him on the excellent burr he had on the letter R.
The seriousness of the situation with regard to our domestic freight rates has been brought home to us very forcibly during the past few months, particularly as it affects our coarse grains in western Canada. The reduction in the price of grains has emphasized in no uncertain way the present cost of freight rates. When the prices of grain were higher and our grain was moving more freely into export, we were not concerned with the freight question to the degree that we are to-day, so far as our feed grains, particularly western barley, are concerned. But now that tariffs have been imposed against our grain going into those countries that import grain, we find
the situation quite different, and it is for that reason that we are obliged to view the whole subject from a slightly different angle.
If I understand correctly the policy of the Conservative party, it is Canada first. We 'farmers in the west have feed grain for sale, and the live stock and poultry producers in both eastern and western Canada want this grain. Now, if the Conservative party are consistent and desire to carry out their policy of Canada first, I should thinik that this is one of the matters that would receive their very earnest consideration, and that early action would be taken in the matter. The hon. member for New Westminster has discussed the matter particularly from the point of view of the poultry producers of British Columbia and also as it affects the live stock feeders. I desire to discuss it from the point of view of the producers in western Canada, [DOT]and, as well, of the feeders in the east.
The question of domestic freight rates is of special interest to the province of Manitoba. Manitoba is one of the oldest of the three western provinces and, as one might 'naturally expect, the fertility of its soil i3 somewhat impaired. We are therefore obliged to turn more towards the production of coarse 'grains, particularly barley. The significance of the situation, so far as Manitoba is concerned, lies in the fact that practically half the barley grown in the three western provinces is grown in that province. Consequently this question is of far-reaching importance to us.
