maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) who has made this motion. Freight rates are always a matter of interest in western Canada. In fact, there is no set of farmers in the
[Mr. W. G. Weir.)
world who are so much interested in freight rates as the farmers of western Canada. Geographically we are situated in the middle of a continent, and the result is that on any produce we have to sell we have to pay a long freight haul to get it to the markets of the world, and on anything we buy, no matter whether we buy it in eastern Canada or elsewhere, we have to pay a long freight haul. If we want to buy lumber, we have to pay a long freight haul from the Pacific coast. If we want to buy fruit, we have to pay a long freight haul from the Pacific coast. On everything that we consume in western Canada, whether manufactured or raw products, we have to pay a long freight haul before we can get it, and on anything that we produce we have to pay a long freight haul before we can get it to the markets of the world. Naturally, therefore, Mr. Speaker, no other people in the world are so interested in rates as the farmers and people of western Canada.
Speaking in this house the other day cn the question of wheat, I pointed out that it costs the farmer of western Canada from 15 to 20 cents a bushel more than any other farmer to get his wheat on the markets of the world. We have a long freight haul to put our wheat on the markets of the world which costs from 30 to 35 cents a bushel, whereas the Argentine, Russia and Australia can put their wheat on the markets of the world at a cost of from 15 to 20 cents a bushel. So there is always in their favour, on account of their having water haul instead of rail haul, an advantage of from 15 to 20 cents a bushel.
Freight rates have always been a burden. Therefore we appreciated very much the action that was taken some years ago when the Crowsnest pass rate was granted. It is onljr in the present year practically, when we have such a quantity of feed and coarse grains that we are not able to get a price for, that we have realized that our local domestic rates are too high as compared with our export rates. As has been pointed out in this debate, we find that in shipping for export, we can ship our barley and coarse grains via Vancouver to Shanghai for a far less rate than we can ship them to Vancouver. We find that the people of Vancouver can practically go to Shanghai and buy Canadian barley there and ship it back to Vancouver, and in the end get it as cheap as if they bought it direct from the prairies. This does not seem right because we are asking the people of British Columbia to produce

Grain Rates-Mr. Donnelly
eggs and poultry, and yet we are sending our coarse grains over to China and Japan to be used by the farmers there in producing poultry and eggs which will compete with the products of our own people. We are giving the farmers of China and Japan cheaper feed than our own people in British Columbia. That surely is not the Canada-first policy. I say that the Canada-first policy is a good policy when not carried to extremes, but I say that in all cases we should help our own Canadians just as much as outsiders, and if we are going to give the people of China and Japan our coarse grains and other products cheaper than we give them to our own people in British Columbia I say that we are not using our own people right.
Again, with regard to grain coming to eastern Canada, we have been told here this afternoon that we are laying our barley down in Hamburg, Copenhagen and other European ports cheaper than in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. We have been told that we are sending our barley and oats and feed wheat to people over there in Europe to feed their hogs and cattle, which are then sold in England in competition with our own hogs and cattle, cheaper than we are sending them to eastern Canada. Surely that is not a Canada first policy. Canadians should get their feeds just as cheap as the people over in Copenhagen and Hamburg and other European ports. In western Canada at the present time we have all kinds of barley and rye and feed oats and feed wheat in storage, and we cannot sell it. Let me give a few illustrations. A man, R. Christie, of Grenfell, had a carload of rye which he shipped to Fort William. When it got there he had a freight bill of $18.35 to pay. So he gave the rye away, and had to pay S18.35 besides to get somebody to take it. Here is another case. C. Bohn of Broadview, had three carloads of rye in the elevator ready to ship. He was preparing to ship when the elevator man said, "I won't ship that out; you have a carload of your good wheat; go to the bank and draw money on that to pay your freight." He went up to the bank and tried to draw money, but the bank would not advance any, and the result was that he had to take the rye back home again or give it away. These are conditions which exist in the west in regard to feed, showing how plentiful and cheap it really, is. In the prairie provinces a certain amount of barley and feed has been sold. Our governments out there pay half the freight rates to different parts. I myself sold some grain which was shipped from one section of Saskatchewan to another half the freight being paid by our local government. In that way we were able to get rid of some of our wheat. In the same way, if the domestic freight rates were cheaper in Saskatchewan the farmers in the western provinces would be able to ship their feed from one part to another, and produce hogs to sell on the markets of the world.
When I was in' the west in the month of December I had presented to me another startling illustration concerning freight rates. At that time No. 1 northern wheat, the best in the world, was selling on the street for 30 cents a bushel. Imagine, No. 1 northern wheat at 30 cents a bushel, half a cant a pound. On the very same day I went down to the premises of one of the milling companies,- the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, to be exact,-and I found that they asked $15 a ton for bran, or three-quarters of a cent a pound. We are paying $15 a ton for bran and selling No. 1 northern wheat for $10 a ton. In other words it required a ton and a half of the best wheat to buy a ton of bran. The same statement applies to flour. In western Canada we grow the wheat, and yet our flour is as highly priced as it is in other parts of the Dominion. Flour in the province of Saskatchewan, where the wheat is grown, is more highly priced than it is in most other parts of Canada or the British Isles. The reason is that no matter where the flour is milled the price is based on Fort William. The price operates just as though the wheat were shipped to Fort William, milled there and the flour shipped back under local freight rates to the province of Saskatchewan. The local freight rates are so high that in Saskatchewan we pay more for our flour than does any other part of Canada. The same is true with regard to bran. That is why I say it required a ton and a half of No. 1 northern wheat to buy a ton of bran.
I wish to refer to only one more point. The excuse may be put forward that a change in the rates will cost the railways too much money, and that at the present time the railways are not making any money. The statement is made that the railways are from day to day losing money and that a reduction in rates would result not in giving them more business, but in financial embarrassment. The suggestion is made that the rates should be increased rather than decreased. I say that if the rates were reduced the business of the railroads would increase and they would do more business. If their rates were reduced more men would be employed. Under the present rates the cost of rights-of-way are just the same, the costs of facilities are just the same, their cars are in their

Grain Rales-Mr. Nicholson
yards and should be in use. If the rates were reduced they would be in use. The coarse grain from western Canada would find its way into eastern Canada. For the last few years we have been importing from Argentina and the United States somewhere in the neighborhood of 10,000,000 or 15,000,000 bushels of corn to feed the cattle of this country. If thait is so we should put a duty on corn. The freight rates on coarse grains should be reduced so that they may be brought east, at a cheaper rate and be placed in competition with the corn from the Argentine. True some stock raisers say that animals cannot be properly finished without the use of corn. Some people believe that, and I do not think we should reject their views and say that they must do without com. I say however that we should place our barley and coarse grains in eastern Canada at low or moderate rates so that we could compete in price with those of Argentina and the United States, thereby preventing corn from coming into this country. Why should com be brought from the Argentine, thereby helping the Argentine farmers, while our own barley is left to rot out on the prairies? I trust the government will consider the matter of rates, and have it referred to a committee so that before very long some remedial action may be taken for the benefit of the western farmers as well as the feeders in eastern Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The question of freight rates which has been raised in the amendment moved by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) is one of very great importance. At this time I would like to direct a few remarks to some of the statements which have been made with regard to the general question of freight rates, and particularly in relation to the observations of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Donnelly). It has been said that the export freight rate on wheat from western Canada is the highest in the world. It may be true that it costs more to send wheat from western Canada to the European markets than to send it from the Argentine republic, Australia or some country where carriage by water is a predominating factor. However, if hon. members would compare the freight rates from western Canada to the markets ,of the world with the freight rates from the United States over the same distances I think they would learn that Canadian freight rates are as advantageous as those of the United States, if indeed they are not more so. The chief point is as to

whether the domestic and export rates shall 'be equalized. The point arises as to whether the people in British Columbia, for instance, would be prepared to have their export and long haul rates equalized with domestic rates all over Canada thereby bringing the Whole freight structure up to the point where the percentage of cost of moving a carload of similar product in any part of Canada would be equalized on a mileage basis. That virtually is what is asked for. Let me put this question: Would the wheat producer in western Canada be in favour of having export rates applied on wheat from western Canada to Fort William, Vancouver, Quebec, Montreal, St. John, New Brunswick or any other exporting point on the same basis as domestic rates for the same character of product to the people all over Canada? On the other hand would producers of lumber, apples and canned products in British Columbia be prepared to defend a freight structure which would cost them on a mileage basis as much to ship a carload of lumber, a carload of apples, a carload of canned salmon or a carload of eggs from Vancouver to Montreal as it would cost an Ontario farmer or lumberman on the same mileage basis to ship his product to the same market. For the information of hon. gentlemen and in no controversial spirit whatsoever I can tell them this, that you can ship a carload of lumber from a (mill in Vancouver to Montreal cheaper than you can ship the same commodity from a northern Ontario mill to the same market; you can ship a carload of apples 100 miles into the Montreal market for less money than you can ship a carload of apples 25 toiles in Ontario to the same market.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Lumber has an alternative
water haul.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is an alternative water haul. But the same thing applies to Toronto, Buffalo, North Tonawanda, or any other large distributing centre in the east; it is the question of the long haul and the short haul. The cost of shipping feed into Ontario has been discussed. It costs more to ship a carload of mill feed, coarse grains, from Fort William 500 miles to some distributing point in Ontario than it costs to ship wheat from Calgary to St. John, New Brunswick, for export. Would anyone suggest that you bring the export rates up to a basis that would make it possible for the railways to earn a revenue upon which they can live, and have them predicated upon the domestic rates?

Grain Rates-Mr. Nicholson

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But we are asking that the
domestic rates east be on the same basis as the rates west to Port Arthur and Fort William.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The export rate is a
low rate on. every commodity, but we have to bear in mind that we must provide a rate structure that will make it possible for the railways to earn sufficient revenue to pay their operating costs. I am not disputing the difficulties we are under in view of the adverse rates, not at all. But the whole point comes back to this:	Can we ask the
railway commission to create a rate structure that will equalize all rates in Canada without affecting export business? I do not think we can. There may be eases such as my hon. friend has cited this afternoon where some injustice exists, but when we discuss the matter of equalized freight rates throughout the country we are going in the face of what has been clamoured for, particularly by western Canada as long as I can remember anything in regard to freight rates, and that is a cheap rate for the long haul exportable product. My hon. friend from Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) who has just taken his seat referred to the fact that there were products in western Canada that you could not ship into any market where they could be sold at a price that would give back the cost of the freight haul. There are many, many cases of that character in all parts of Ontario. Let me cite just one that I happen to know something about myself. There are 20,000,000 laths in the lumber yards of firms with which I am associated, and there is a market for those laths in New York. It will cost 50 cents a thousand more to ship those laths from the point of production to New York than they can be sold for when they arrive there. That is due to the depressed condition in business of that character all over the world.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Water competition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is due to the tariff.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it is not due to
the tariff either. There is not any tariff applying. We ship the produce free, and if the exporter in the United States could ship it across here it would come in free. The trouble is due to the low value of the product and the cost of haulage. In fact there is virtually no value in the product after the freight is paid. These things apply in a hundred different ways. For example, take the long haul and the preferential freight rate. It will cost a farmer in the Ottawa
Valley more to ship me a carload of potatoes for one of my lumber camps than it will cost the farmer in New Brunswick to ship a carload of potatoes to the same place. If someone suggested that we equalize those rates as between the Ontario and New Brunswick farmers, I am afraid the maritimers in this house would raise the same cry as has been raised in western Canada. Everybody sympathizes with the situation we are in, but when you approach the question of a rate structure based on equalized rates, and say you are going to have the same comparative rate between Alberta and Vancouver as between Alberta and Hong Kong, I am very much afraid you are defeating the very object you are endeavouring to attain in creating an export market for the goods that we produce so largely in this country, and that we must export.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Are we to assume then that export freight rates are not profitable?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the matter was
analyzed from A to Z, it would be found that the railways could not live on export rates; for instance, they could not live on the rates on export wheat from western Canada to the European markets.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There is plenty of
evidence to the contrary on the Crowsnest pass grain rates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the course of that discussion if must be borne in mind that you leave out of the picture entirely the whole capital cost behind the construction of the railways, the maintenance of their equipment and everything else that goes with it- absolutely inescapable charges. If you distributed the export business in grain alone over twelve months of the year, instead of the short period during which grain has to be hauled, you could reduce the rolling stock of all the railways in Canada 50 per cent.
Mr. fl AN BURY: That is true in British Columbia where we have a twelve month period.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why is it true? Because this equipment is idle eight months out of the twelve.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not in British Columbia.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Good
heavens! that is not true.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Excuse me, it is true.
Grain Rates-Mr. Nicholson

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But my
hon. friend can take the actual statistics of the railroads and find that the haulage of wheat continues fairly steadily throughout the year with the exception of the winter months.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It continues, yes, to some degree; but will my hon. friend suggest that ihe statement is not correct, that the period of the year when the heavy wheat traffic prevails is September, October, November and December?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Quite correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And if that traffic was equally distributed over the whole twelve months, I repeat my statement-and I know it to be correct-50 per cent of the rolling stock that has been brought into being in this country for the purpose of carrying that freight would never have been required to be purchased.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But the domestic business is more all-the-year-round than the export; therefore it should get a lower rate.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is perfectly true; if you lower the domestic rate and increase the export rate, and so make it possible for the railways to live, all well and good; but you cannot reduce both sets of rates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If my hon. friend will come to Vancouver he will find that they have seed grain moving every day of the year for export. Our contention is they should reduce the domestic rate and get the resultant increased tonnage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And increase the export rate?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend take the balance sheets of the Canadian National Railways for the last ten years and find out how much money they made on these rates?
Mr. NEILL; They paid 10 per cent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Canadian National Railways?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, the Canadian National Railways.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the domestic rate was reduced the increased volume would mean cheaper haulage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It happened when the differential was cut 50 per cent.	'

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman can make a speech for himself later.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not propose to take up the time of the house very much longer in connection with this matter. I merely rose to point out what was prevailing all over this country. I would point out that if people in the west or in the far east, who are constantly referring to these things, are anxious to have an equalization of freight rates, domestic and export, they should study the problem with some degree of thoroughness before making any suggestion of that kind. I am afraid it would be the people in the west who would suffer to a very great degree.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is not my hon. friend overlooking the fact that the chief contention has been that grain is not moving at all under the existing rates?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is perfectly true; lumber is not moving either, and there are hundreds of commodities which are not moving under the existing rates. Do we suggest that we are going to load the whole thing on the railroads and ask them to carry goods for nothing? That is virtually what it would amount to. As an hon. member suggests, where would they carry those goods? This matter should be left with the railway commission.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have left it with the railway commission too long.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I say to my hon. friend, do not urge too strongly an equalization of short and long haul rates, because it will be the people at the extremities of this country who will suffer most from any such equalization.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up very much of the time of the house, but no hon. member from Alberta has had a chance to say anything as yet in regard to this resolution. I want to assure the hon. member who brought up the matter that he has almost the unanimous support of the people of Alberta in demanding a lower domestic freight rate on grain. Sometimes in my district we have low grade grain which we would like to ship to the poultry-, men of British Columbia, but we cannot do so because of the high freight rate. I have under my hand a letter from the assistant chief traffic officer of the Board of Railway Commissioners, under date of May 2, 1929, in which he says that the rate for export from our station to Vancouver and New West-

Grain Rates-Mr. Coote
minster is 20 cents per hundred pounds, but that the rate on grain for domestic consumption to the same points is 42 cents per hundred pounds or more than double the export rate. The rate to Victoria is 45 cents per hundred pounds, considerably more than double the rate for export.
Just in reply to the remarks of the last speaker may I say that we believe the increased traffic under a lower freight rate on domestic grain would make up for any loss which might be sustained in moving the quantity now being handled at a lower rate. I do not think there is much doubt about that, and we might all receive the benefits of such a reduction. In order to show the house that the farmers of Alberta are solidly behind the people of British Columiba in their efforts to secure a reduction on the rate on domestic grain, I should like to quote a resolution which was passed at the last annual meeting of the United Farmers of Alberta. I think resolutions similar to this have been passed by this organization annually for the past eight or nine years. The resolution reads:
Whereas the freight rate on wheat for domestic use in British Columbia is one hundred per cent higher than the rate on wheat for export:
Be it resolved that we ask the federal government to lower the rate on domestic wheat to the same level as for export wheat.
I should like also to read a resolution passed at a general meeting of the wheat pools of western Canada, held in Winnipeg on March 13:
Whereas, the Canadian surplus of feed grains is increasing year by year due to increased production and the difficulties faced by the Canadian live stock industry; and
Whereas, millions of bushels of Argentine and American corn are imported each year into Canada for feed purposes; and
Whereas, the logical outlet Of large quantities of the surplus feed grains from western Canada lies in the live stock industry of the Dominion: and
Whereas, the domestic market for feed grains is the only sure market in these difficult times; and
"Whereas, there is very marked disparity between domestic and export freight rates on feed grains to the extent that western Canadian barley, for example, has been laid down in such European ports as Hamburg, Bremen, Antwerp, Rotterdam. Copenhagen and Liverpool at from six to thirteen cents per bushel cheaper than the same grain could be supplied to feeders of live stock in the maritimes of Canada;
Be it therefore resolved, that this interprovincial conference, representative of the pool grain marketing agencies in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, go on record as strongly urging the necessity for a thorough investigation into this disparity in domestic and export freight rates on -western grain, both east and west, with a view to bringing about
an equalization of such rates; and that copies of this resolution be forwarded to the governments of Canada and of all the provinces, the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, and also to each member of the House of Commons.
I believe that resolution expresses very clearly and very fairly the opinion of the grain growers of western Canada in regard to this matter. I had intended to quote some of the actual rates in effect between different points, but that has been so well covered by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Weir) that I will not bother to do so at this time. However, I do wish to say that I think it is time the government of Canada took some action-because we cannot get action from the railway commission-to see that the egg producers of Japan and the bacon producers of Denmark do not secure Canadian grain for less than is paid by Canadian producers of these same commodities.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would my hon. friend suggest that we should abolish the railway commission and make the whole question of freight rates in this country a political question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I will not go that far
at present, but I never could understand some of the .judgments of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Just here I should like to say a word of appreciation of the work of Hon. Air. Oliver, a former member of that board. I should like to quote very briefly from the dissenting judgment rendered by Mr. Oliver in connection with this very matter under discussion. He said:
The all-rail export rate Fort William to Montreal is 34J cents per 100 pounds. The domestic rate is 37i cents which is three cents over the export rate. The rail distance Fort William to Montreal is somewhat more than one-half greater than that between Calgary and Vancouver. There would not appear to be any reason why the difference between export and domestic rates on grain of export standards from prairie points to Vancouver should be greater than that between domestic and export rates on the longer haul, Fort William to Montreal.
If the domestic rate on grain coming east *is only three cents per bushel more than the 'export rate, why should it be more than double on grain going west? That is what 'we cannot understand. The judgment pro-[DOT]ceeds:
Although a domestic rate three cents per 100 pounds over the export rate from prairie points to Vancouver would be the same difference between domestic and export rates as now prevails on the all-rail grain movement from Fort William to Montreal, it would not put the respective populations of Vancouver and Montreal in the same relative positions as to cost of their domestic supplies, because central
Grain Rates-Mr. Coote

Canada generally, including Montreal, in fact gets the bulk of its domestic supply by rail and water at the export rate.
Then Mr. Oliver goes on to deal with the question of damaged grain:
Damaged grain is not as suitable feed for live stock as sound grain, but if it can be secured at a sufficiently lower price, it answers the purpose fairly well and will be used accordingly. The present domestic rate of 41J cents per 100 pounds practically excludes such grain from use by the poultry and dairy farmers of the coast region and compels them either to pay the full price for grain of export quality, with the 41J cent transportation cost added, or to buy corn imported by ship from the Argentine. Either way the country suffers an economic loss and their difficulties in carrying on their operations are materially increased.
I commend that paragraph to the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson). It explains the case fairly well, and indicates why the domestic rate should be lowered. Then again:	[DOT]
The feed value of low grade or damaged grain is not sufficient to allow the British Columbia consumer to pay a price that will enable the producer to haul to the railway station and pay the present domestic rail rate as well, in competition with corn from the Argentine, delivered by ship in Vancouver. The railroad therefore altogether loses the haul on this grain, while the producer loses the selling value of the grain and the British Columbia poultry and dairy farmer pays his money for a foreign supply. . . . The transportation of grain of these lower grades at export rates would not by any means place the consuming population of British Columbia in the same favourable position in regard to their domestic food and feed supply as that at present enjoyed by the people of central Canada, but it would be in that direction and would be of substantial advantage to the prairie producer and to the railway as well.
I should like to quote the last two sentences of his judgment. He recommends:
That the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways be notified that rates on grain and flour for domestic use shall not be more than 3 cents per 100 pounds higher from prairie points to Vancouver than the rates from the same points on grain and flour for export.
He does not suggest the same rates, but he does suggest that the same rate might apply 'on low grade grain.
Provided that the rate on grain below export quality, that is, wheat of a quality below the grade of No. 4 northern, and other grains below the grade of No. 3 C.W. (Canada Western) shall not exceed the export rate.
I am quite unable to understand why the other commissioners should, not have agreed *with the judgment given by Mr. Oliver. It 'seems to me to have been reasonable. I would simply say in closing that I hope the government will take such action as may be necessary to adjust this situation. Certainly it

should be remedied, and in my -opinion such 'action would be as fine a part of the Canada First policy as this government could possibly take.

maintopic: SUPPLY-GRAIN RATES AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I want to endorse what has been said in regard to this question. I am in sympathy with the suggestion that something should be done in connection with this domestic rate problem. The time is ripe for it, and now that the matter has been submitted to the Prime Minister I am sure something will ibe done. I trust it will not be a football for years to come but that we shall get results.
On motion of Mr. Willis the debate was adjourned.

At six o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
